claim: Damage to the primary visual cortex (V1) causes hemianopia.
source: Although damage to the primary visual cortex (V1) causes hemianopia, many patients retain some residual vision; known as blindsight.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Many patients with V1 damage retain some residual vision known as blindsight.
source: Although damage to the primary visual cortex (V1) causes hemianopia, many patients retain some residual vision; known as blindsight.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is the basis for the study.

claim: Blindsight may be facilitated by an intact white-matter pathway between the lateral geniculate nucleus and motion area hMT+.
source: We show that blindsight may be facilitated by an intact white-matter pathway between the lateral geniculate nucleus and motion area hMT+.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by psychophysical and tractography data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: All blindsight positive individuals showed intact geniculo-hMT+ pathways.
source: All blindsight positive individuals showed intact geniculo-hMT+ pathways, while this pathway was significantly impaired or not measurable in blindsight negative individuals.
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data presented in Table 1 and Figures 2-4.

claim: The geniculo-hMT+ pathway was significantly impaired or not measurable in blindsight negative individuals.
source: All blindsight positive individuals showed intact geniculo-hMT+ pathways, while this pathway was significantly impaired or not measurable in blindsight negative individuals.
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography and microstructure data in Table 1, Figures 2-4, and statistical analyses.

claim: The superior colliculus to hMT+ pathway was not consistently present in blindsight positive cases.
source: Two white matter pathways previously implicated in blindsight: (i) superior colliculus to hMT+ and (ii) between hMT+ in each hemisphere were not consistently present in blindsight positive cases.
evidence: This is supported by the tractography data in Table 1 showing variable presence of this pathway.

claim: The pathway between hMT+ in each hemisphere was not consistently present in blindsight positive cases.
source: Two white matter pathways previously implicated in blindsight: (i) superior colliculus to hMT+ and (ii) between hMT+ in each hemisphere were not consistently present in blindsight positive cases.
evidence: This is supported by the tractography data in Table 1 showing this pathway was present in only 6/12 blindsight positive patients.

claim: The study included 17 patients with V1 damage acquired during adulthood.
source: Visual psychophysics, diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging and fibre tractography were applied in 17 patients with V1 damage acquired during adulthood and 9 age-matched controls.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and participant numbers.

claim: The study included 9 age-matched controls.
source: Visual psychophysics, diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging and fibre tractography were applied in 17 patients with V1 damage acquired during adulthood and 9 age-matched controls.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and participant numbers.

claim: Several visual pathways have been proposed to underlie blindsight over the past 30 years.
source: Over the past 30 years, several visual pathways have been proposed to underlie this residual vision, but the relative role of these pathways and the neurobiological bases for blindsight remains unknown (see Cowey, 2010 for review).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The relative role of visual pathways and the neurobiological bases for blindsight remains unknown.
source: Over the past 30 years, several visual pathways have been proposed to underlie this residual vision, but the relative role of these pathways and the neurobiological bases for blindsight remains unknown (see Cowey, 2010 for review).
evidence: This is stated as the knowledge gap that motivates the study, supported by citation.

claim: Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging combined with tractography offers a practical and non-invasive method for estimating large-scale white matter tracts in living humans.
source: Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) combined with tractography offers a practical and non-invasive method for estimating large-scale white matter tracts and studying their microstructural properties in living humans (Johansen-Berg, 2010; Catani et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Intact ipsilateral white matter connecting lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) and extrastriate cortex, specifically area hMT+, has been proposed as a candidate circuit that could support blindsight.
source: Using dMRI in a number of individual patients, intact ipsilateral white matter connecting lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) and extrastriate cortex, specifically area hMT+, has been proposed as a candidate circuit that could support blindsight (de Gelder et al., 2008; Bridge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The macaque LGN can support residual visual processing after V1 lesion.
source: In agreement with this proposal, the macaque LGN can support residual visual processing after V1 lesion (Schmid et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a macaque study.

claim: Blindsight may result from visual plasticity to strengthen interhemispheric white matter in humans.
source: Two alternative proposals suggest blindsight results either from visual plasticity, for example to strengthen interhemispheric white matter in humans (Leh et al., 2006; Bridge et al., 2008; Tamietto et al., 2012) or intact connections to hMT+ from the superior colliculus and pulvinar, demonstrated in the macaque (Warner et al., 2010, 2015).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Blindsight may result from intact connections to hMT+ from the superior colliculus and pulvinar.
source: Two alternative proposals suggest blindsight results either from visual plasticity, for example to strengthen interhemispheric white matter in humans (Leh et al., 2006; Bridge et al., 2008; Tamietto et al., 2012) or intact connections to hMT+ from the superior colliculus and pulvinar, demonstrated in the macaque (Warner et al., 2010, 2015).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis supported by citations to macaque studies.

claim: The superior colliculus has been implicated in human residual vision after V1 damage, particularly for indirect blindsight and saccadic localisation.
source: The superior colliculus has also been implicated in human residual vision after V1 damage, particularly for indirect blindsight and saccadic localisation (Mohler and Wurtz, 1977; Leh et al., 2006; Kato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The necessary circuitry supporting preserved vision after V1 damage in humans has not been identified prior to this study.
source: To date the necessary circuitry supporting preserved vision after V1 damage in humans has not been identified.
evidence: This is stated as the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: The study investigated visual white matter tracts in the largest group of patients measured to date with chronic unilateral V1 damage sustained in adulthood.
source: The present study investigated visual white matter tracts in the largest group of patients measured to date with chronic unilateral V1 damage sustained in adulthood (n = 17, see Supplementary file 1 for clinical and demographic details) and healthy age-matched controls (n = 9).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and its novelty.

claim: The large subject group enabled the division of patients into those demonstrating blindsight and those who did not.
source: The large subject group enabled the division of patients into those demonstrating blindsight, and those who did not.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design enabled by the sample size.

claim: The preservation or destruction of the geniculate-hMT+ tract predicted presence or absence of blindsight respectively.
source: The preservation or destruction of the geniculate-hMT+ tract predicted presence or absence of blindsight respectively.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the tractography and behavioral data.

claim: The geniculate-hMT+ tract was reliably identified in all blindsight positive patients.
source: More specifically, the geniculate-hMT+ tract was reliably identified in all blindsight positive patients, but was impossible to track or showed considerably impaired white matter microstructure in all blindsight negative individuals.
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: The geniculate-hMT+ tract was impossible to track or showed considerably impaired white matter microstructure in all blindsight negative individuals.
source: More specifically, the geniculate-hMT+ tract was reliably identified in all blindsight positive patients, but was impossible to track or showed considerably impaired white matter microstructure in all blindsight negative individuals.
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography and microstructure data in Table 1 and Figures 2-4.

claim: The two alternative candidate tracts (collicular-hMT+ and interhemispheric hMT+) showed variable predominance in both patient groups.
source: In contrast, the two alternative candidate tracts showed variable predominance in both patient groups and therefore seem unlikely to underlie blindsight function.
evidence: This is supported by the tractography data in Table 1 and Figure 5.

claim: The alternative candidate tracts seem unlikely to underlie blindsight function.
source: In contrast, the two alternative candidate tracts showed variable predominance in both patient groups and therefore seem unlikely to underlie blindsight function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variable presence of these tracts across patient groups.

claim: Twelve patients were classified as 'blindsight positive'.
source: Based on these criteria, 12 were classified as 'blindsight positive' and this relatively sensitive binary measure allowed us to be confident that patients labelled as 'blindsight negative' (n = 5) showed no residual visual function.
evidence: This is directly stated based on the psychophysical testing results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Five patients were classified as 'blindsight negative'.
source: Based on these criteria, 12 were classified as 'blindsight positive' and this relatively sensitive binary measure allowed us to be confident that patients labelled as 'blindsight negative' (n = 5) showed no residual visual function.
evidence: This is directly stated based on the psychophysical testing results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No patients could describe the stimulus in their blind field.
source: No patients could describe the stimulus in their blind field, although the degree of awareness varied from a complete absence of awareness to an appreciation of motion at times in the minority of cases.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the behavioral testing.

claim: Two different classification algorithms agreed with the distinction based on performance at 100% contrast in all cases.
source: Both classification algorithms agree with the distinction based on performance in 100% contrast in all cases.
evidence: This validates the classification method using cross-validation approaches.

claim: All 12 blindsight positive patients had ipsilateral, uncrossed tracts between the LGN and hMT+.
source: All 12 blindsight positive patients and the 9 age-matched controls were found to have ipsilateral, uncrossed tracts between the LGN and hMT+.
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: All 9 age-matched controls had ipsilateral, uncrossed tracts between the LGN and hMT+.
source: All 12 blindsight positive patients and the 9 age-matched controls were found to have ipsilateral, uncrossed tracts between the LGN and hMT+.
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: The number of fascicles measured was of similar magnitude in control and blindsight positive individuals.
source: The number of fascicles measured was of similar magnitude in control and blindsight positive individuals.
evidence: This is supported by the fascicle count data in Table 1.

claim: There was considerable variation in fascicle numbers between participants and between hemispheres.
source: As expected (Jones et al., 2013; Pestilli et al., 2014), even after cleaning, there was considerable variation in fascicle numbers between participants and, in some cases, between hemispheres although this variability was similar for controls (range = 19–653) and patients (range = 17–635).
evidence: This is directly observed in the data and supported by citations indicating this is expected.

claim: It was possible to track a pathway between the LGN and hMT+ in the damaged hemisphere of 4/5 blindsight negative patients.
source: In blindsight negative patients it was possible to track a pathway between the LGN and hMT+ in the damaged hemisphere of 4/5 patients (we failed to identify the tract in PN4), with a similar number of fascicles to blindsight positive patients (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: All blindsight negative patients with trackable LGN-hMT+ pathways showed considerable abnormality in the microstructure of these tracts compared to their intact hemisphere or control participants.
source: However, all of these patients showed considerable abnormality in the microstructure of these tracts compared to their intact hemisphere or control participants, highlighting the importance of considering white matter microstructure in patient tractography studies.
evidence: This is supported by the FA and MD data shown in Figures 2B and 3B.

claim: Mean FA in blindsight positive patients was 0.43 ± 0.05 in the damaged hemisphere and 0.49 ± 0.05 in the intact hemisphere for the geniculate-hMT+ pathway.
source: Mean FA, calculated across all blindsight positive patients and collapsed along the whole geniculate-hMT+ pathway, was 0.43 ± 0.05 (mean ± s.d.) in the damaged hemisphere and 0.49 ± 0.05 in the intact hemisphere, corresponding to a laterality of 13.7% (see Figure 2B and 'Materials and methods' for details).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: The laterality in FA for the geniculate-hMT+ pathway in blindsight positive patients was 13.7%.
source: Mean FA, calculated across all blindsight positive patients and collapsed along the whole geniculate-hMT+ pathway, was 0.43 ± 0.05 (mean ± s.d.) in the damaged hemisphere and 0.49 ± 0.05 in the intact hemisphere, corresponding to a laterality of 13.7% (see Figure 2B and 'Materials and methods' for details).
evidence: This is calculated from the FA measurements.

claim: Mean FA in blindsight negative patients was 0.35 ± 0.1 on the ipsilesional side vs 0.47 ± 0.03 in the intact hemisphere for the geniculate-hMT+ pathway.
source: In blindsight negative patients (Figure 2B, middle column), the microstructure of ipsilesional tracts was particularly abnormal. Mean FA was 0.35 ± 0.1 (mean ± s.d.) on the ipsilesional side, vs 0.47 ± 0.03 in the intact hemisphere (laterality = 34.7%).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: The laterality in FA for the geniculate-hMT+ pathway in blindsight negative patients was 34.7%.
source: Mean FA was 0.35 ± 0.1 (mean ± s.d.) on the ipsilesional side, vs 0.47 ± 0.03 in the intact hemisphere (laterality = 34.7%).
evidence: This is calculated from the FA measurements.

claim: Control participants show a left-right laterality of 3.3% for FA in the geniculate-hMT+ pathway.
source: In comparison, control participants (Figure 2B, right column) show a left-right laterality of 3.3% for FA (range = 0.3–0.66. Mean FA = 0.51 ± 0.03 left, 0.49 ± 0.03 right hemisphere) and 1.6% for MD (range = 0.56 x 10−3–0.91 x 10−3, Mean MD = 0.73 x 10−3 ± 0.03 x 10−3 left, 0.72 x 10−3 ± 0.03 x 10−3 right hemisphere).
evidence: This is calculated from the FA measurements in control participants.

claim: Control participants show a left-right laterality of 1.6% for MD in the geniculate-hMT+ pathway.
source: In comparison, control participants (Figure 2B, right column) show a left-right laterality of 3.3% for FA (range = 0.3–0.66. Mean FA = 0.51 ± 0.03 left, 0.49 ± 0.03 right hemisphere) and 1.6% for MD (range = 0.56 x 10−3–0.91 x 10−3, Mean MD = 0.73 x 10−3 ± 0.03 x 10−3 left, 0.72 x 10−3 ± 0.03 x 10−3 right hemisphere).
evidence: This is calculated from the MD measurements in control participants.

claim: Mean MD in blindsight positive cases was 0.81 x 10−3 ±0.07 x 10−3 in the damaged hemisphere and 0.73 x 10−3 ±0.05 x 10−3 in the intact hemisphere for the geniculate-hMT+ pathway.
source: In blindsight positive cases, mean MD was 0.81 x 10−3 ±0.07 x 10−3 in the damaged hemisphere, and 0.73 x 10−3 ±0.05 x 10−3 in the intact hemisphere (laterality = 9.6%).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: The laterality in MD for the geniculate-hMT+ pathway in blindsight positive patients was 9.6%.
source: In blindsight positive cases, mean MD was 0.81 x 10−3 ±0.07 x 10−3 in the damaged hemisphere, and 0.73 x 10−3 ±0.05 x 10−3 in the intact hemisphere (laterality = 9.6%).
evidence: This is calculated from the MD measurements.

claim: Blindsight negative patients had a mean MD of 1.05 x 10−3 ±0.22 x 10−3 in the damaged hemisphere compared to 0.77 x 10−3 ± 0.05 x 10−3 on the intact side for the geniculate-hMT+ pathway.
source: Conversely, blindsight negative patients had a mean MD of 1.05 x 10−3 ±0.22 x 10−3 in the damaged hemisphere, compared to 0.77 x 10−3 ± 0.05 x 10−3 on the intact side, representing a laterality of 27.0%.
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: The laterality in MD for the geniculate-hMT+ pathway in blindsight negative patients was 27.0%.
source: Conversely, blindsight negative patients had a mean MD of 1.05 x 10−3 ±0.22 x 10−3 in the damaged hemisphere, compared to 0.77 x 10−3 ± 0.05 x 10−3 on the intact side, representing a laterality of 27.0%.
evidence: This is calculated from the MD measurements.

claim: There was no significant effect of blindsight status on FA values within the geniculate-hMT+ tract (F = 2.6, p = 0.13).
source: While there was no significant effect of blindsight status (positive or negative; F = 2.6, p = 0.13), there was a highly significant effect of lesion side (ipsilateral or contralateral; F = 35.7; p < 0.00005) and interaction, suggesting a differential effect of the lesion in the two patient groups (F = 5.1; p = 0.04).
evidence: This is the result of a two-way ANOVA statistical test on the FA data.

claim: There was a highly significant effect of lesion side on FA values within the geniculate-hMT+ tract (F = 35.7; p < 0.00005).
source: While there was no significant effect of blindsight status (positive or negative; F = 2.6, p = 0.13), there was a highly significant effect of lesion side (ipsilateral or contralateral; F = 35.7; p < 0.00005) and interaction, suggesting a differential effect of the lesion in the two patient groups (F = 5.1; p = 0.04).
evidence: This is the result of a two-way ANOVA statistical test on the FA data.

claim: There was a significant interaction effect on FA values within the geniculate-hMT+ tract, suggesting a differential effect of the lesion in the two patient groups (F = 5.1; p = 0.04).
source: While there was no significant effect of blindsight status (positive or negative; F = 2.6, p = 0.13), there was a highly significant effect of lesion side (ipsilateral or contralateral; F = 35.7; p < 0.00005) and interaction, suggesting a differential effect of the lesion in the two patient groups (F = 5.1; p = 0.04).
evidence: This is the result of a two-way ANOVA statistical test on the FA data.

claim: There was a significant effect of blindsight status on MD values within the geniculate-hMT+ tract (F = 9.2; p < 0.01).
source: This effect was even stronger for MD: significant effect of blindsight status (F = 9.2; p < 0.01), significant effect of lesion side (F = 35.7; p < 0.00005) and interaction (F = 12.4; p < 0.005).
evidence: This is the result of a two-way ANOVA statistical test on the MD data.

claim: There was a significant effect of lesion side on MD values within the geniculate-hMT+ tract (F = 35.7; p < 0.00005).
source: This effect was even stronger for MD: significant effect of blindsight status (F = 9.2; p < 0.01), significant effect of lesion side (F = 35.7; p < 0.00005) and interaction (F = 12.4; p < 0.005).
evidence: This is the result of a two-way ANOVA statistical test on the MD data.

claim: There was a significant interaction effect on MD values within the geniculate-hMT+ tract (F = 12.4; p < 0.005).
source: This effect was even stronger for MD: significant effect of blindsight status (F = 9.2; p < 0.01), significant effect of lesion side (F = 35.7; p < 0.00005) and interaction (F = 12.4; p < 0.005).
evidence: This is the result of a two-way ANOVA statistical test on the MD data.

claim: Estimates of distinct pathways frequently overlapped.
source: Since estimates of distinct pathways frequently overlapped (Figure 3A), the slight laterality in patients may, at least in part, be driven by an overlap with degenerated optic radiations supplying damaged V1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and discussed as a potential confound.

claim: The slight laterality in patients may be driven by overlap with degenerated optic radiations supplying damaged V1.
source: Since estimates of distinct pathways frequently overlapped (Figure 3A), the slight laterality in patients may, at least in part, be driven by an overlap with degenerated optic radiations supplying damaged V1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed overlap shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the central nervous system, anterograde (Wallerian) or retrograde neuronal degeneration can occur following axonal injury.
source: In the central nervous system, anterograde (Wallerian) or retrograde neuronal degeneration can occur following axonal injury.
evidence: This is stated as established neurobiological knowledge.

claim: The integrity of optic radiation fibres innervating damaged V1 would be abnormal throughout their course.
source: Consequently, the integrity of optic radiation fibres innervating damaged V1 would be abnormal throughout their course (similar to Danek et al., 1990).
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of Wallerian degeneration, supported by citation.

claim: dMRI measurements would not distinguish between separate axonal bundles due to limitations in spatial resolution restricted to 2 mm isotropic voxel size.
source: Where overlap with such fibres occurs, the dMRI measurements would not distinguish between separate axonal bundles due to limitations in spatial resolution (restricted here to 2 mm isotropic voxel size).
evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of the imaging method.

claim: Mean FA in blindsight positive patients in the distal portion of the geniculate-hMT+ pathway was 0.39 ± 0.06 in the damaged hemisphere and 0.42 ± 0.04 in the intact hemisphere.
source: Mean FA in blindsight positive patients was 0.39 ± 0.06 in the damaged hemisphere and 0.42 ± 0.04 in the intact hemisphere, corresponding to a laterality of only 7.7% (mean MD = 0.79 x 10−3 ± 0.06 x 10−3 vs 0.73 x 10−3 ± 0.06 x 10−3, laterality = 7.6%).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data for the distal portion of the tract.

claim: The laterality in FA for the distal portion of the geniculate-hMT+ pathway in blindsight positive patients was 7.7%.
source: Mean FA in blindsight positive patients was 0.39 ± 0.06 in the damaged hemisphere and 0.42 ± 0.04 in the intact hemisphere, corresponding to a laterality of only 7.7% (mean MD = 0.79 x 10−3 ± 0.06 x 10−3 vs 0.73 x 10−3 ± 0.06 x 10−3, laterality = 7.6%).
evidence: This is calculated from the FA measurements for the distal portion.

claim: Mean FA in the distal portion of the geniculate-hMT+ tract in blindsight negative patients was 0.29 ± 0.07 compared to 0.44 ± 0.05 in the intact hemisphere.
source: In blindsight negative patients, mean FA in the distal portion of this tract was 0.29 ± 0.07, compared to 0.44 ± 0.05 in the intact hemisphere (laterality = 51.7%), mean MD = 1.04 x 10−3 ± 0.23 x 10−3 vs 0.74 x 10−3 ± 0.07 x 10−3, (laterality = 28.8%).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data for the distal portion of the tract.

claim: The laterality in FA for the distal portion of the geniculate-hMT+ pathway in blindsight negative patients was 51.7%.
source: In blindsight negative patients, mean FA in the distal portion of this tract was 0.29 ± 0.07, compared to 0.44 ± 0.05 in the intact hemisphere (laterality = 51.7%), mean MD = 1.04 x 10−3 ± 0.23 x 10−3 vs 0.74 x 10−3 ± 0.07 x 10−3, (laterality = 28.8%).
evidence: This is calculated from the FA measurements for the distal portion.

claim: The effect of blindsight status on mean FA within the distal portion of the geniculate-hMT+ tract was not significant (F = 0.7; p = 0.42).
source: Although the effect of blindsight status on mean FA within this distal portion was not significant (F = 0.7; p = 0.42), both the effect of lesion side (F = 48.6; p < 0.00001) and the interaction (F = 15.6; p < 0.0005) were highly significant.
evidence: This is the result of a statistical test on the distal portion FA data.

claim: The effect of lesion side on mean FA within the distal portion of the geniculate-hMT+ tract was highly significant (F = 48.6; p < 0.00001).
source: Although the effect of blindsight status on mean FA within this distal portion was not significant (F = 0.7; p = 0.42), both the effect of lesion side (F = 48.6; p < 0.00001) and the interaction (F = 15.6; p < 0.0005) were highly significant.
evidence: This is the result of a statistical test on the distal portion FA data.

claim: The interaction effect on mean FA within the distal portion of the geniculate-hMT+ tract was highly significant (F = 15.6; p < 0.0005).
source: Although the effect of blindsight status on mean FA within this distal portion was not significant (F = 0.7; p = 0.42), both the effect of lesion side (F = 48.6; p < 0.00001) and the interaction (F = 15.6; p < 0.0005) were highly significant.
evidence: This is the result of a statistical test on the distal portion FA data.

claim: The effect of blindsight status on mean MD within the distal portion of the geniculate-hMT+ tract was significant (F = 7.9; p = 0.01).
source: The effect of blindsight status on mean MD was significant (F = 7.9; p = 0.01), as were the effect of lesion side (F = 31.4; p < 0.0001) and the interaction (F = 15.6; p = 0.001).
evidence: This is the result of a statistical test on the distal portion MD data.

claim: The effect of lesion side on mean MD within the distal portion of the geniculate-hMT+ tract was significant (F = 31.4; p < 0.0001).
source: The effect of blindsight status on mean MD was significant (F = 7.9; p = 0.01), as were the effect of lesion side (F = 31.4; p < 0.0001) and the interaction (F = 15.6; p = 0.001).
evidence: This is the result of a statistical test on the distal portion MD data.

claim: The interaction effect on mean MD within the distal portion of the geniculate-hMT+ tract was significant (F = 15.6; p = 0.001).
source: The effect of blindsight status on mean MD was significant (F = 7.9; p = 0.01), as were the effect of lesion side (F = 31.4; p < 0.0001) and the interaction (F = 15.6; p = 0.001).
evidence: This is the result of a statistical test on the distal portion MD data.

claim: Only blindsight negative patients possess tracts in the damaged hemisphere that appear to traverse a region of white matter displaying very abnormal FA and MD levels.
source: Only the blindsight negative patients (Figure 4, lower portion) possess tracts in the damaged hemisphere that appear to traverse a region of white matter displaying very abnormal FA and MD levels.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 comparing blindsight positive and negative patients.

claim: There was no significant effect of blindsight status on grey matter volume in hMT+ (F = 0.1; p = 0.8).
source: There was no significant effect of blindsight status (F = 0.1; p = 0.8), lesion side (F = 1.7; p = 0.2) or interaction (F = 1.0; p = 0.3), indicating that differences in grey matter volume within hMT+ are unlikely to have affected the results significantly.
evidence: This is the result of a statistical test on grey matter volume data.

claim: There was no significant effect of lesion side on grey matter volume in hMT+ (F = 1.7; p = 0.2).
source: There was no significant effect of blindsight status (F = 0.1; p = 0.8), lesion side (F = 1.7; p = 0.2) or interaction (F = 1.0; p = 0.3), indicating that differences in grey matter volume within hMT+ are unlikely to have affected the results significantly.
evidence: This is the result of a statistical test on grey matter volume data.

claim: Differences in grey matter volume within hMT+ are unlikely to have affected the results significantly.
source: There was no significant effect of blindsight status (F = 0.1; p = 0.8), lesion side (F = 1.7; p = 0.2) or interaction (F = 1.0; p = 0.3), indicating that differences in grey matter volume within hMT+ are unlikely to have affected the results significantly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical tests showing no significant effects.

claim: Interhemispheric hMT+ tracts were identified in only 6/12 patients with blindsight.
source: Crossing tracts between hMT+ bilaterally were identified in only 6/12 patients with blindsight and 6/9 controls (Table 1, columns 3–4).
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: Interhemispheric hMT+ tracts were identified in 6/9 controls.
source: Crossing tracts between hMT+ bilaterally were identified in only 6/12 patients with blindsight and 6/9 controls (Table 1, columns 3–4).
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: Interhemispheric hMT+ pathways always crossed to the opposite hemisphere via the corpus callosum.
source: As expected, pathways always crossed to the opposite hemisphere via the corpus callosum (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A-C and is consistent with anatomical knowledge.

claim: Mean FA for interhemispheric hMT+ tracts in blindsight positive cases was 0.64 ± 0.07.
source: In blindsight positive cases, mean FA was 0.64 ± 0.07 (mean ± s.d.) and mean MD 0.70 x 10−3 ±0.03 x 10−3, averaged along the entire tract for both directions (left to right, and right to left), and across participants (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: Mean MD for interhemispheric hMT+ tracts in blindsight positive cases was 0.70 x 10−3 ±0.03 x 10−3.
source: In blindsight positive cases, mean FA was 0.64 ± 0.07 (mean ± s.d.) and mean MD 0.70 x 10−3 ±0.03 x 10−3, averaged along the entire tract for both directions (left to right, and right to left), and across participants (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: Mean FA for interhemispheric hMT+ tracts in controls was 0.64 ± 0.07.
source: These values were similar to controls (Figure 6C, mean FA = 0.64 ± 0.07, mean MD = 0.67 x 10−3 ±0.05 x 10−3).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: Mean MD for interhemispheric hMT+ tracts in controls was 0.67 x 10−3 ±0.05 x 10−3.
source: These values were similar to controls (Figure 6C, mean FA = 0.64 ± 0.07, mean MD = 0.67 x 10−3 ±0.05 x 10−3).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: Only a single blindsight negative patient (PN2) showed an interhemispheric connection between hMT+ bilaterally.
source: Only a single blindsight negative patient showed an interhemispheric connection between hMT+ bilaterally (PN2; Table 1, Figure 5B), and in this case, the tract appeared to be largely intact and remained within the control FA range (0.28–0.91), with mean FA = 0.59 and MD = 0.73 x 10−3 (see Figure 6B for FA plots along this path).
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: The interhemispheric hMT+ tract in patient PN2 appeared to be largely intact and remained within the control FA range.
source: Only a single blindsight negative patient showed an interhemispheric connection between hMT+ bilaterally (PN2; Table 1, Figure 5B), and in this case, the tract appeared to be largely intact and remained within the control FA range (0.28–0.91), with mean FA = 0.59 and MD = 0.73 x 10−3 (see Figure 6B for FA plots along this path).
evidence: This is based on the FA and MD measurements for this patient shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Collicular-hMT+ pathways were tracked in the damaged hemisphere of 8/12 blindsight positive patients.
source: Specifically, these pathways were tracked in the damaged hemisphere of 8/12 blindsight positive patients (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: The collicular-hMT+ pathway was present in 3/5 blindsight negative patients.
source: In comparison, this pathway was present in 3/5 blindsight negative patients (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: Control participants showed collicular-hMT+ pathways in all nine cases on the left and 7/9 on the right.
source: Control participants showed these pathways in all nine cases on the left, and 7/9 on the right (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is directly supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: Mean FA for the collicular-hMT+ pathway in blindsight positive patients was 0.40 ± 0.05 in the damaged hemisphere vs 0.46 ± 0.03 on the intact side.
source: Of the patients demonstrating this pathway, mean FA was 0.40 ± 0.05 in the damaged hemisphere of blindsight positive cases, vs 0.46 ± 0.03 on the intact side, with some regions of overlap along their trajectory (laterality of 13.9%, see Figure 6D for FA plots).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: The laterality in FA for the collicular-hMT+ pathway in blindsight positive patients was 13.9%.
source: Of the patients demonstrating this pathway, mean FA was 0.40 ± 0.05 in the damaged hemisphere of blindsight positive cases, vs 0.46 ± 0.03 on the intact side, with some regions of overlap along their trajectory (laterality of 13.9%, see Figure 6D for FA plots).
evidence: This is calculated from the FA measurements.

claim: Mean MD for the collicular-hMT+ pathway in blindsight positive patients was 0.78 x 10−3 ± 0.08 x 10−3 vs 0.69 x 10−3 ±0.04 x 10−3.
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: The laterality in MD for the collicular-hMT+ pathway in blindsight positive patients was 10.8%.
evidence: This is calculated from the MD measurements.

claim: Mean FA for the collicular-hMT+ pathway in blindsight negative patients was 0.37 ± 0.05 vs 0.42 ± 0.03 on the intact side.
source: Collapsed along the pathway, mean FA was 0.37 ± 0.05 vs 0.42 ± 0.03 on the intact side (laterality = 14.0%), and MD was 0.83 x 10−3 x 10−3 ±0.13 vs 0.77 x 10−3 ±0.07 x 10−3 (laterality = 7.5%).
evidence: This is directly measured from the diffusion MRI data.

claim: The laterality in FA for the collicular-hMT+ pathway in blindsight negative patients was 14.0%.
source: Collapsed along the pathway, mean FA was 0.37 ± 0.05 vs 0.42 ± 0.03 on the intact side (laterality = 14.0%), and MD was 0.83 x 10−3 x 10−3 ±0.13 vs 0.77 x 10−3 ±0.07 x 10−3 (laterality = 7.5%).
evidence: This is calculated from the FA measurements.

claim: Intact tracts from the superior colliculus can occur in blindsight negative patients.
source: This implies that intact tracts from the superior colliculus can occur in blindsight negative patients.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that two blindsight negative patients (PN2 and PN3) showed similar microstructure in both hemispheres for the collicular tract.

claim: There was no significant difference in FA or MD in the ipsilesional collicular-hMT+ hemisphere between blindsight positive and negative groups.
source: However, a comparison of FA and MD in just the ipsilesional hemisphere indicated no significant difference in either measure between the two groups (FA: t = 0.9; p = 0.4; d.f. = 9; MD: t = 0.8; p = 0.45; d.f. = 9).
evidence: This is the result of statistical tests comparing the two groups.

claim: The correlation between percentage of correct responses and FA in the distal geniculate-hMT+ tract was not significant (r = 0.44; p = 0.09).
source: Although both correlations were in the predicted direction, positive for FA and negative for MD, neither was significant (r = 0.44; p = 0.09 for FA; r = −0.48; p = 0.06 for MD).
evidence: This is the result of a correlation analysis between behavior and tract microstructure.

claim: The correlation between percentage of correct responses and MD in the distal geniculate-hMT+ tract was not significant (r = −0.48; p = 0.06).
source: Although both correlations were in the predicted direction, positive for FA and negative for MD, neither was significant (r = 0.44; p = 0.09 for FA; r = −0.48; p = 0.06 for MD).
evidence: This is the result of a correlation analysis between behavior and tract microstructure.

claim: Neither the collicular-hMT+ nor the interhemispheric hMT+ tracts showed any correlation with behaviour.
source: Neither the collicular-hMT+ (r = −0.03; p = 0.93 for FA; r = −0.10; p = 0.77 for MD) nor the interhemispheric hMT+ (r = −0.33; p = 0.39 for FA; r = 0.26; p = 0.50 for MD) tracts showed any correlation with behaviour.
evidence: This is the result of correlation analyses between behavior and tract microstructure.

claim: Average lesion volume in the blindsight positive group was 13,461 mm3 ± 7101 mm3 s.d.
source: Average lesion volume in the blindsight positive group was 13,461 mm3 ± 7101 mm3 s.d., compared to 36,923 mm3 ± 23,035 s.d. in the blindsight negative group.
evidence: This is directly measured from the lesion masks created from T1 structural scans.

claim: Average lesion volume in the blindsight negative group was 36,923 mm3 ± 23,035 s.d.
source: Average lesion volume in the blindsight positive group was 13,461 mm3 ± 7101 mm3 s.d., compared to 36,923 mm3 ± 23,035 s.d. in the blindsight negative group.
evidence: This is directly measured from the lesion masks created from T1 structural scans.

claim: Blindsight negative patients had lesions approximately 2.5 times larger than the blindsight positive group on average.
source: On average, blindsight negative patients had lesions approximately 2.5 times larger than the blindsight positive group, although Figure 8B shows the overlap of occipital lobe damage between patients.
evidence: This is calculated from the lesion volume measurements.

claim: There was a significant association between the extent of occipital lobe damage and the microstructural measures of ipsilesional geniculate-hMT+ pathways across all patients.
source: There was a significant association between the extent of occipital lobe damage and the microstructural measures of ipsilesional geniculate-hMT+ pathways across all patients (FA: r = −0.59, p = 0.015; MD: r = 0.63, p = 0.01).
evidence: This is the result of correlation analyses between lesion extent and tract microstructure.

claim: There was no clear association between blindsight function and the presence of additional, non-occipital damage.
source: There was no clear association between blindsight function and the presence of additional, non-occipital damage.
evidence: This is an observation based on the lesion location data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Only one participant (PN5) showed evidence of significant subcortical pathology.
source: Furthermore, only one participant showed evidence of significant subcortical pathology (PN5), seen to extend to a region including the ipsilesional LGN and pulvinar, although the superior colliculi appeared intact.
evidence: This is based on examination of the lesion masks and anatomical images.

claim: At least three patients with blindsight showed complete destruction of calcarine cortex or its underlying white matter.
source: At least three patients with blindsight showed complete destruction of calcarine cortex or its underlying white matter (PB1, PB4, PB10).
evidence: This is based on examination of the lesion masks and anatomical images.

claim: There were blindsight negative cases with small regions of V1 apparently intact.
source: Similarly there were blindsight negative cases with small regions of V1 apparently intact (PN2, PN4).
evidence: This is based on examination of the lesion masks and anatomical images.

claim: This is the first study to perform dMRI-based tractography and a comparison of the microstructural tissue properties of visual pathways in a group of patients with V1 damage, categorised according to blindsight function.
source: This is the first study to perform dMRI-based tractography and a comparison of the microstructural tissue properties of visual pathways in a group of patients with V1 damage, categorised according to blindsight function.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study design.

claim: All patients with blindsight function showed intact, undamaged tracts between the LGN and hMT+ in the hemisphere with V1 damage.
source: The principal finding was that all patients with blindsight function showed intact, undamaged tracts between the LGN and hMT+ in the hemisphere with V1 damage.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the tractography and microstructure data.

claim: The finding of intact LGN-hMT+ pathways in blindsight positive patients is consistent with a recent fMRI report of motion processing after V1 damage.
source: This is consistent with our recent fMRI report of motion processing after V1 damage (Ajina et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the same authors.

claim: A similar direct geniculate pathway was identified in all age-matched controls.
source: A similar direct geniculate pathway was identified in all age-matched controls, and is consistent with neuroanatomical investigation in the macaque (Sincich et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the tractography data and citation to macaque anatomy.

claim: The direct geniculate pathway is consistent with neuroanatomical investigation in the macaque.
source: A similar direct geniculate pathway was identified in all age-matched controls, and is consistent with neuroanatomical investigation in the macaque (Sincich et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a macaque study.

claim: Intact connections between the LGN and hMT+ may be sufficient for blindsight.
source: It is possible that intact connections between the LGN and hMT+ are sufficient for blindsight, since no patients with blindsight function demonstrated an absence or impairment in these pathways.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that all blindsight positive patients had intact LGN-hMT+ pathways.

claim: Intact connections between the LGN and hMT+ may be necessary for blindsight function.
source: Intact connections between the LGN and hMT+ may also be necessary for blindsight function. This is supported by the results in blindsight negative patients, as none of the patients without blindsight function possessed normal, intact connections in this pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that no blindsight negative patients had intact LGN-hMT+ pathways.

claim: It is possible that other, unexplored pathways could also underlie blindsight function in blindsight negative patients.
source: However, since the current study only investigated a limited number of potential pathways, it is possible that other, unexplored, pathways could also underlie blindsight function in these patients.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative explanations not tested in the study.

claim: There were examples of patients with blindsight function who had absent or impaired collicular and interhemispheric pathways.
source: Unlike direct geniculate connections, there were examples of patients with blindsight function who had absent or impaired collicular and interhemispheric pathways.
evidence: This is supported by the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: There were blindsight negative cases with apparently undamaged connections between the superior colliculus and hMT+ or between hMT+ bilaterally.
source: Similarly, there were blindsight negative cases with apparently undamaged connections between these regions.
evidence: This is supported by the tractography and microstructure data in Table 1 and Figures 5-6.

claim: Neither the collicular nor interhemispheric pathways have a major role in blindsight function.
source: These results suggest that neither of these other putative blindsight pathways have a major role in blindsight function, but support the argument that in blindsight positive cases, another pathway must have facilitated visual performance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variable presence of these pathways across patient groups.

claim: The collicular and interhemispheric pathways may still contribute to blindsight in some circumstances.
source: However, these pathways may still contribute to blindsight in some circumstances.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential roles not definitively ruled out by the data.

claim: The most commonly described pulvinar pathway is a di-synaptic pathway from colliculus to hMT+ via the inferior pulvinar.
source: Firstly, the most commonly described pathway is a di-synaptic pathway from colliculus to hMT+ via the inferior pulvinar (Lyon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A direct, retinorecipient pathway from the inferior pulvinar has been described in the marmoset.
source: A direct, retinorecipient pathway from the inferior pulvinar has been described in the marmoset (Warner et al., 2010), suggesting that it would also be worth considering only a connection between inferior pulvinar and hMT+.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a marmoset study.

claim: A recent human tractography study found that tracts from both LGN and pulvinar to hMT+ were very similar with almost identical values for both FA and MD.
source: A recent human tractography study considered tracts from both LGN and pulvinar to hMT+ as part of an investigation into the visual pathways in amblyopia (Allen et al., 2015). Quantification of the tract microstructure found that they were very similar with almost identical values for both FA and MD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: At the current resolution of 2 mm isotropic voxels, dissecting apart LGN-hMT+ and pulvinar-hMT+ tracts may be impossible due to the proximity of the thalamic structures.
source: Thus, at the current resolution of 2 mm isotropic voxels, dissecting apart these two tracts may be impossible, due to the proximity of the thalamic structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical limitations of the imaging method and cited previous work.

claim: The study cannot completely rule out the presence of an intact direct pathway from the retina to hMT+ via the pulvinar.
source: Thus, we cannot completely rule out the presence of an intact direct pathway from the retina to hMT+ via the pulvinar.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging a limitation of the study.

claim: Patient GY showed a direct ipsilateral connection between LGN and hMT+ in the damaged hemisphere.
source: The motion study reported a direct ipsilateral connection between LGN and hMT+ in the damaged hemisphere, similar to the results for blindsight positive patients here.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous case study.

claim: Patient GY showed unusual patterns of connectivity that may be indicative of plasticity.
source: However, GY also showed unusual patterns of connectivity that may be indicative of plasticity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from a previous case study.

claim: Only patients with blindsight following hemispherectomy showed crossing tracts between the superior colliculus in the damaged hemisphere and regions of the intact hemisphere.
source: Only patients with blindsight showed crossing tracts between the superior colliculus in the damaged hemisphere and regions of the intact hemisphere, as well as strong ipsilateral connections in the damaged hemisphere.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The current study found no evidence to support plasticity in adult-onset V1 damage and blindsight.
source: The current study found no evidence to support such plasticity in adult-onset V1 damage and blindsight.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of unusual connectivity patterns in the current patient cohort.

claim: Where occipital damage is bilateral, the corpus callosum undergoes profound degeneration and is unlikely to provide useful visual information.
source: Where occipital damage is bilateral, the corpus callosum undergoes profound degeneration and is unlikely to provide useful visual information (de Gelder et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The age of brain injury onset may explain differences in plasticity, since damage acquired in childhood may lead to greater plastic changes.
source: One possible explanation for some of these differences is the age of brain injury onset, since damage acquired in childhood may lead to greater plastic changes (Anderson et al., 2011; Tinelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous studies on developmental plasticity.

claim: Patient GY sustained his brain injury aged 8 years.
source: GY sustained his brain injury aged 8 years, and the hemispherectomy patients sustained severe structural brain damage at birth or in early childhood, despite undergoing resective surgery later in life.
evidence: This is factual information about a previously studied patient.

claim: The hemispherectomy patients sustained severe structural brain damage at birth or in early childhood.
source: GY sustained his brain injury aged 8 years, and the hemispherectomy patients sustained severe structural brain damage at birth or in early childhood, despite undergoing resective surgery later in life.
evidence: This is factual information about previously studied patients.

claim: Increased interhemispheric connectivity in blindsight could be consistent with an increased propensity for plasticity in the corpus callosum.
source: Both studies identified increased interhemispheric connectivity in blindsight, unlike the cases of cortical blindness and patients in the current study, all of whom sustained damage in adulthood. This could be consistent with an increased propensity for plasticity in the corpus callosum, which continues to grow in cross-sectional area until early adulthood (Keshavan et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to developmental neuroscience literature.

claim: Different forms of blindsight may be mediated by distinct anatomical pathways or structures.
source: It has been argued in the past that different forms of blindsight may be mediated by distinct anatomical pathways or structures (Danckert and Rossetti, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous theoretical paper.

claim: Collicular processing may be involved in 'action' or 'attention' blindsight.
source: For example, collicular processing may be involved in 'action' or 'attention' blindsight, whilst the LGN is implicated in perceptual characteristics, described as 'agnosopsia' (Zeki and Ffytche, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The LGN is implicated in perceptual characteristics of blindsight, described as 'agnosopsia'.
source: For example, collicular processing may be involved in 'action' or 'attention' blindsight, whilst the LGN is implicated in perceptual characteristics, described as 'agnosopsia' (Zeki and Ffytche, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: It was possible to track robust fascicles in patients traversing regions of extremely impaired FA and MD.
source: A significant concern highlighted from the current study is that it was possible to track robust fascicles in patients traversing regions of extremely impaired FA and MD.
evidence: This is an observation from the tractography results, particularly in blindsight negative patients.

claim: Fascicles may be biased towards narrow regions of white matter running alongside a lesion boundary.
source: Indeed, it may even be the case that fascicles are biased towards narrow regions of white matter running alongside a lesion boundary.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential artifact in tractography algorithms.

claim: Patient PN1 showed almost ten times more fascicles in the geniculate-hMT+ pathway of his damaged hemisphere compared to his intact side.
source: Patient PN1, for example, showed almost ten times more fascicles in the geniculate-hMT+ pathway of his damaged hemisphere compared to his intact side, even though tracts quite clearly passed through a region of abnormal (damaged) tissue (Figure 4).
evidence: This is directly observed in the tractography data shown in Table 1 and Figure 4.

claim: Tracts in patient PN1 are unlikely to be functional, as indicated by the negative psychophysical performance.
source: These tracts are unlikely to be functional, as indicated by the negative psychophysical performance.
evidence: This is an inference combining tractography and behavioral data.

claim: Emphasis on fascicle numbers without considering the underlying microstructure and pathway viability is problematic.
source: Emphasis on fascicle numbers without considering the underlying microstructure and pathway viability is therefore problematic.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of trackable but non-functional pathways.

claim: There are many reasons why fascicle numbers provide unreliable measures of true axonal projections and function.
source: Indeed, there are many reasons why fascicle numbers provide unreliable measures of true axonal projections and function (Jones et al., 2013; Pestilli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methodological papers.

claim: The number of reconstructed fascicles may differ due to the length, curvature, and degree of branching present even if the 'true' fibre count is uniform.
source: Even if the 'true' fibre count is uniform, the number of reconstructed fascicles may differ due to the length, curvature, and degree of branching present (Jones and Cercignani, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a methodological paper.

claim: Control participants showed notable differences in fascicle numbers between hemispheres and individuals.
source: Such variability was apparent here, as even control participants showed notable differences in fascicle numbers between hemispheres and individuals.
evidence: This is directly observed in the tractography data in Table 1.

claim: False positive connections are particularly problematic in using MRI diffusion tractography to comment on the existence or absence of a specific pathway.
source: One of the more controversial uses of MRI diffusion tractography is to comment on the existence or absence of a specific pathway, with false positive connections particularly problematic (Sherbondy et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methodological papers.

claim: A less stringent cut-off in the cleaning process would suggest collicular tracts were present in all blindsight positive patients.
source: Although the interhemispheric and geniculate pathways in patients would remain unaffected, a less stringent cut-off would suggest collicular tracts were present in all blindsight positive patients.
evidence: This is a speculation about how methodological choices affect results.

claim: Pathways containing fewer than 5 fascicles appear largely implausible when visualized.
source: However, when visualized, these pathways containing fewer than 5 fascicles appear largely implausible, reinforcing the need for a cleaning process to improve data reliability and reduce false positives.
evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection of the tractography results.

claim: Linear Fascicle Evaluation may be a novel mechanism to estimate the accuracy of an estimated connectome and tract in the future.
source: A novel mechanism to address this in the future may be to estimate the accuracy of an estimated connectome and tract, such as using Linear Fascicle Evaluation (Pestilli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future methodological improvements, supported by citation.

claim: This work provides strong evidence to support a direct geniculate connection to extrastriate cortex as being important for blindsight function in adult-onset V1 damage.
source: In summary this work provides strong evidence to support a direct geniculate connection to extrastriate cortex as being important for blindsight function in adult-onset V1 damage.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the tractography and behavioral data.

claim: Alternate interhemispheric and collicular pathways were unable to account for all blindsight cases.
source: Although alternate interhemispheric and collicular pathways were also demonstrable in a number of patients, these connections were unable to account for all blindsight cases and were often found to be intact in patients with absent blindsight performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the variable presence of these pathways across patient groups.

claim: Alternate pathways were often found to be intact in patients with absent blindsight performance.
source: Although alternate interhemispheric and collicular pathways were also demonstrable in a number of patients, these connections were unable to account for all blindsight cases and were often found to be intact in patients with absent blindsight performance.
evidence: This is supported by the tractography data showing these pathways in some blindsight negative patients.

claim: The results highlight the importance of considering white matter microstructure when performing tractography in patients.
source: The results also highlight the importance of considering white matter microstructure when performing tractography in patients, which is applicable to anyone working with clinical diffusion data.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion drawn from the observation that fascicle counts alone were insufficient.

claim: Appreciation of the important tracts may help to direct attempts to boost residual function through rehabilitative strategies in hemianopia.
source: Finally, appreciation of the important tracts may help to direct attempts to boost residual function through rehabilitative strategies in hemianopia.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications of the findings.

claim: Fifteen patients had sustained posterior circulation stroke.
source: Seventeen patients (five female) took part in this study, of which 15 had sustained posterior circulation stroke and two had undergone benign tumour resection, see Supplementary file 1 for details.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the patient cohort.

claim: Two patients had undergone benign tumour resection.
source: Seventeen patients (five female) took part in this study, of which 15 had sustained posterior circulation stroke and two had undergone benign tumour resection, see Supplementary file 1 for details.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the patient cohort.

claim: All patients had sustained unilateral damage to V1, causing homonymous visual field loss recorded by Humphrey perimetry.
source: All patients had sustained unilateral damage to V1, causing homonymous visual field loss recorded by Humphrey perimetry.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the inclusion criteria for the patient cohort.

claim: Average age of patients at the time of participation was 54.9 years ± 14.4.
source: Average age at the time of participation was 54.9years ± 14.4, average time after pathology onset 45 months (range 6–252 months).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the patient demographics.

claim: Average time after pathology onset was 45 months (range 6–252 months).
source: Average age at the time of participation was 54.9years ± 14.4, average time after pathology onset 45 months (range 6–252 months).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the patient demographics.

claim: Control participants and patients were matched by age and sex at the time of testing.
source: Control participants and patients were matched by age and sex at the time of testing.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design.

claim: Controls all had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity and no history of neurological disease.
source: Controls all had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity and no history of neurological disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the inclusion criteria for control participants.
